sections.h2: How is Richmond, Virginia, divided, and what does that mean for a house sale?
sections.html:
Richmond is usually described in four parts: the North Side, Southside, East End and West End. Each has its own housing mix, from Victorian townhouses to mid-century ranches, so the story of a Richmond house depends heavily on which side of the James River it is on.

The city is Virginia's capital and its fourth most populous city. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 237,257 residents, up from 226,610 in the 2020 census. Richmond has been an independent city since 1871, so there is no county layer between you and city hall.

Richmond's original street grid dates to 1737 and covered the area between today's Broad, 17th and 25th streets and the river. Modern downtown sits slightly west of that, on the slopes of Shockoe Hill.

  • East End: includes Church Hill, home to St. John's Church, along with Fulton, Union Hill and Fairmount.
  • The Fan and Museum District: the area between the Boulevard, Main Street and Broad Street, with Monument Avenue and many Victorian buildings, next to the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts.
  • Carytown: the commercial strip along Cary Street between Interstate 195 and the Boulevard.
  • North Side: many listed historic districts, including Ginter Park, Barton Heights, Highland Park and Chestnut Hill-Plateau, developed after the streetcar arrived.
  • West End: suburban in feel, with Windsor Farms among its best-known sections.
  • Southside: Westover Hills, Forest Hill, Woodland Heights, Stratford Hills and Old Town Manchester, among others.

The Southside has a different history from the rest of the city. Richmond absorbed the former city of Manchester in 1910, and on January 1, 1970 the city grew south by 27 square miles and gained 47,000 residents, after Chesterfield County lost a court fight against the annexation.

sections.h2: What jobs support the Richmond housing market?
sections.html:
Law, finance and government drive the Richmond economy. The downtown area holds federal, state and local agencies along with large law and banking firms, and the city is one of about a dozen with both a U.S. Court of Appeals and a Federal Reserve Bank.

The Richmond metro area includes several Fortune 500 companies: Performance Food Group, Altria, CarMax, Dominion Energy, Markel, Owens and Minor, Genworth Financial and ARKO Corp. Capital One also has significant offices in the city.

Health and research add to this mix. Virginia Commonwealth University and its Medical College of Virginia campus anchor the Virginia BioTechnology Research Park, which opened in 1995 and has more than 575,000 square feet of lab and office space.

With that range of employers, a seller of a damaged or dated house is often weighing the cost of repairs against simply selling as is. We can give you a clear answer on the second option without any pressure.

It can. The James River reaches tidewater at Richmond, and flooding may happen in any month, most often in March and least often in July.

Hurricanes and tropical storms have caused most summer and early fall floods. Three hurricanes in 1955, including Connie and Diane, produced record rainfall over six weeks, and in 2004 the remnants of Hurricane Gaston dropped up to 12 inches of rain and caused extensive damage downtown.

A multimillion-dollar flood wall was completed in 1995 to protect the low-lying parts of the city from the rising river. Shockoe Bottom, the low area between Shockoe Hill and Church Hill, is described as historically significant and low-lying.

  • Before listing, check whether your lot sits in a mapped floodplain.
  • Walk the basement or lowest floor for stains, mold or a sump pump that no longer works.
  • Gather any insurance or repair records tied to past water damage.

sections.h2: What winter and summer weather should Richmond sellers plan for?
sections.html:
Richmond has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and moderately cold winters. Snow averages 10.5 inches a season, and snow usually stays on the ground only a day or two.

There are exceptions. Snow stayed 16 days in early 2010 and 17 days in 2026, from January 25 to February 10. Ice storms are not unusual, though they are seldom severe enough to cause widespread damage, and tornadoes are infrequent.

For a seller, older roofs, gutters and pipes in unheated vacant houses are the usual pressure points. A vacant house in a cold snap can turn a small plumbing issue into a large repair bill.

sections.h2: Which courts and agencies are based in Richmond?
sections.html:
Richmond is home to the Supreme Court of Virginia, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, one of the four divisions of the Eastern District of Virginia and one of the four divisions of its Bankruptcy Court.

For sellers, this matters in two ways. State agencies and courts mean the capital has a large base of public employees, and it also means legal help for probate, title or bankruptcy questions is close at hand. If your sale involves an estate, ask the local circuit court clerk what filings are needed before a deed can be signed.

sections.h2: How do roads and the river shape commutes?
sections.html:
Richmond's downtown has long been a hub: boats at the Great Turning Basin, rail with one of only two triple rail crossings in North America, and two intersecting major interstates. Interstates 95, 64 and 195 all touch the city's neighborhoods.

The distance to jobs matters in this area. Richmond is about 21 miles north of Petersburg and part of the larger Richmond-Petersburg metro area, which includes surrounding counties such as Chesterfield, Henrico and Hanover.

When you describe your house, mention the nearest interstate access, the side of the river it is on and how far it is from VCU or downtown, since those details drive how buyers see it.

sections.h2: What does a Richmond seller pay at closing?
sections.html:
Virginia's grantor tax is 50 cents for each $500 of the sale price, paid by the seller unless the buyer agrees to cover it. The clerk must certify the tax before the deed can be recorded, and the state and locality split the proceeds equally.

See Virginia Code 58.1-802 for the wording. For assessment cycles, tax rates, due dates and appeal deadlines, contact the city's real estate assessor and finance office for current numbers before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for a Richmond house?
sections.html:
A Richmond cash sale uses the same Virginia contract, title and deed steps as a financed sale, without a lender waiting on an appraisal. That shortens the timeline and removes one of the most common reasons deals fall apart.

Send us the address and a few details about condition and timing. We review it, and if an offer fits, it covers the house as it is. You do not clean out, repair or stage, and you can decline without owing anything.

This route is worth a look if you are an heir, a landlord or an owner of a worn house anywhere from the Southside to the East End and you want a firm closing date.

faqs.q: What is the population of Richmond, VA?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimates 237,257 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 226,610 in 2020.

faqs.q: Does the James River flood in Richmond?
faqs.a: Yes. Flooding can occur in any month, most often in March, and a flood wall was completed in 1995 to protect low-lying areas.

faqs.q: When did Richmond grow south into Southside?
faqs.a: On January 1, 1970, the city annexed 27 square miles from Chesterfield County, adding about 47,000 residents.

faqs.q: Who pays the Virginia grantor tax in a Richmond sale?
faqs.a: The seller, at 50 cents per $500 of the price, unless the buyer agrees to pay some or all of it.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Richmond house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase it as is, so you do not have to make repairs first.

faqs.q: Which large employers are near Richmond?
faqs.a: The metro area includes Performance Food Group, Altria, CarMax, Dominion Energy, Markel, Owens and Minor, Genworth Financial and ARKO Corp.
